Exterior Painting Guide

Exterior Painting in Porirua: What Coastal Weather Does to Your Paint, and How to Make It Last

Porirua is a hard place for exterior paint. Salt air, strong southerly wind and long wet winters wear it down faster than in a sheltered inland town. A repaint here is not just a colour change. It is protection for the cladding, timber and framing underneath, and this guide explains what the weather does to paint here, which surfaces suffer most, what a proper job includes, and what it should cost.

Salt air wears paint out first

Porirua is a coastal city, and homes near the harbour and the open coast sit in salty air every day. Salt settles on paint, draws in moisture and speeds up wear, especially on weatherboards and metal fittings. A home in Titahi Bay facing the sea will usually need its paint checked sooner than a similar home further inland, and the same problem shows up in Plimmerton and along the harbour.

Salt does its worst work where paint is already thin or cracked. Once moisture gets behind it, the peeling spreads, so a small patch of flaking paint on a coastal wall is worth fixing early.

Wind pushes rain into every gap

Strong southerly winds are the second problem. They drive rain into cracks, joints and gaps around windows and doors, and if the paint has already cracked, rain gets behind it and the damage grows. Good preparation matters as much as the paint itself: sealing gaps, priming bare timber and applying two full coats help keep moisture out.

Rain works with the other two. Wellington rain can keep a house damp through winter, feeding mould, moss and lichen on shaded walls, while summer sun fades dark colours. A well-prepared repaint lasts 7 to 10 years. Exposed coastal homes may need repainting sooner, sheltered homes can last longer.

Which cladding suffers most

Not every wall in Porirua fails the same way. The cladding decides what goes wrong and what paint it needs.

CladdingWhat goes wrongWhat it needs
Timber weatherboardsPeeling, cracking and rot where water gets inScrape, fill, sand, prime bare timber, two coats of flexible exterior acrylic
Monolithic, stucco and renderCracks, water uptake and mould on shaded wallsClean, repair cracks, treat mould, masonry paint that lets moisture out
Brick and fibre cementPaint lifting at joints and fixings as sheets moveCorrect primer and masonry paint, joints checked before painting
Fascia, eaves and trimPeeling edges where rain runs off the roofSand, fill, prime, durable trim enamel in two coats

Weatherboards are the most common cladding on Porirua homes, especially houses built in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s. Timber moves with temperature, so the paint on it needs to move too, and a flexible exterior acrylic is the usual choice. Monolithic and rendered walls are the opposite: plaster or cement that can take in water and grow mould, so their paint has to let moisture out while stopping rain getting in, and cracks must be repaired first or the paint bubbles and peels. If a rendered wall needs replastering before it can be painted, it helps to know the difference between traditional plastering vs modern skim coating first, since the repair underneath decides how well the paint on top holds.

Preparation is most of the job

Every exterior job in Porirua should start with a proper house wash. Water blasting removes dirt, salt, mould, moss and loose paint from the walls, eaves and paths. Paint sticks far better to a clean surface, and washing also reveals problems that need fixing before painting, like cracks, rotten boards and damaged seals.

After washing comes the slow work: scrape off loose paint, sand smooth, fill gaps and cracks, repair damaged boards and prime bare areas. Only then do two full coats of premium exterior paint go on, with fascia, eaves and trim finished in enamel.

Our guide to preparing a house for painting in Porirua's coastal climate walks through each stage, from washing and scraping to priming and the final walk-through.

Paint, colour and finish

Most exterior work in Porirua uses good quality New Zealand paint brands, such as Resene and Dulux, chosen for the cladding and how much weather each wall faces. Cheap paint often needs more coats and wears out faster in sun and salt air, while a good paint with UV protection, flexibility and mould resistance costs more per litre and lasts longer.

Colour matters too. Light shades reflect heat and can make a property look brighter, while dark colours give a modern look but show fading sooner in strong sun. Warm whites with dark trim suit many Porirua homes, and soft greys work well on coastal weatherboard properties.

Before you decide, test your colours on the actual walls. Natural light, shade and wall size all change how a colour looks next to a small paint chart. A free colour consultation, with test patches checked in morning and evening light, is part of a proper exterior painting in Porirua service, and the final choice is always yours.

What it costs, and what changes the price

For a standard 3-bedroom weatherboard home, a full exterior repaint in Porirua usually costs between $8,000 and $15,000. A free, detailed quote is the number that matters, and it should list preparation, repairs, paint and labour separately.

Six things move the price most: house size and storeys, cladding type and condition, preparation work, access, paint quality, and trim and deck work. Bigger homes need more paint, hours and sometimes scaffolding, damaged walls add preparation, and premium paint costs more per litre but often needs fewer coats and lasts longer.

Affordable exterior painting does not mean rushing the job or skipping preparation. A rushed job that starts peeling after two years can cost more to fix than a proper job that lasts ten. If you are comparing quotes, ask every painter three questions: what preparation work is included, what type and quality of paint will be used, and is the quote fixed and in writing. A suburb-by-suburb Porirua house painting checklist by suburb can help you work through what your own home needs before you ask for quotes.

Mistakes that shorten a paint job

Skipping preparation

Painting over dirt, salt, mould or loose paint is the main reason new paint starts peeling. Always wash, scrape, fill, sand and prime first.

Painting over mould

Mould must be treated before painting, or it can grow back through the new paint.

One thick coat

One thick coat leaves runs and spots that wear out faster. Two full coats give a smoother finish and last longer.

Wrong paint for the cladding

Standard wall paint on stucco, or interior paint outside, will not last. Use paint made for the surface.

Two more mistakes are easy to make in Porirua. Painting in rain or strong wind stops paint settling properly, and painting cold or damp surfaces stops paint sticking, so winter work needs planning around dry weather.

The verdict for Porirua homes

If your home sits near the coast, treat exterior paint as protection first and decoration second. Wash and prepare properly, match the paint to the cladding and use two coats of good quality exterior paint. Done that way, a repaint should last 7 to 10 years. Done in a rush, it can fail in two.

Frequently asked questions

How long does exterior paint last in Porirua?

A well-prepared repaint lasts around 7 to 10 years. Exposed coastal homes may need repainting sooner.

How much does it cost to paint the outside of a house in Porirua?

A full exterior repaint for a standard 3-bedroom weatherboard home usually costs between $8,000 and $15,000, depending on size, cladding, condition, access and paint quality.

Can you paint over mould?

No. Mould must be treated before painting. If you paint over it without treating it first, it can grow back through the new paint.
